content: 1. Guiding Principles and Recommendations from the 2010 WHO Guidelines on HIV and Infant Feeding: Infant feeding practices for mothers living with HIV should prioritize the highest likelihood of HIV-free survival for their children while ensuring the health of the mother is not compromised. This principle remains valid. National health authorities should integrate HIV testing, care, and treatment interventions for all women into maternal and child health services. This integration is essential and remains a valid recommendation. National or subnational health authorities should decide whether to counsel and support HIV-positive mothers to either breastfeed with antiretroviral (ARV) drug interventions or avoid breastfeeding entirely, depending on which strategy offers the best chance of HIV-free survival for infants. This recommendation remains valid. In situations where ARV drugs are not immediately available, breastfeeding may still provide HIV-exposed infants with a better chance of HIV-free survival. Efforts should be made to accelerate access to ARV drugs for maternal health and prevention of HIV transmission to infants. This principle remains valid. Even in the absence of ARV drugs, mothers should be counseled to exclusively breastfeed for the first six months of life and continue breastfeeding thereafter unless replacement feeding is safe and feasible. In emergencies where ARV drugs are unavailable, breastfeeding is recommended to improve infant survival. This has been updated to a formal recommendation and remains valid. Mothers who are HIV-negative or whose HIV status is unknown should be counseled to exclusively breastfeed for the first six months, introduce complementary foods thereafter, and continue breastfeeding for up to 24 months or beyond. HIV testing should be offered to mothers with unknown status. This recommendation remains valid. 2. Recommendations for Breastfeeding Practices and Duration: In settings where national authorities promote breastfeeding with ARV interventions as the primary strategy for HIV-free survival, mothers living with HIV (whose infants are HIV-negative or of unknown status) should exclusively breastfeed for the first six months, introduce appropriate complementary foods thereafter, and continue breastfeeding for the first 12 months. The 2016 guidelines revised the recommended duration of breastfeeding and HIV treatment. 3. Guidance for Mothers Who Decide to Stop Breastfeeding: HIV-positive mothers who choose to stop breastfeeding should do so gradually over one month. If the mother or infant has been receiving ARV prophylaxis, it should continue for one week after breastfeeding cessation. However, lifelong antiretroviral therapy (ART) is now recommended instead of ARV prophylaxis. 4. Feeding Infants After Breastfeeding Cessation: For infants under six months, alternatives include commercial infant formula or expressed, heat-treated breast milk. Home-modified animal milk is not recommended for infants under six months. For children older than six months, alternatives include commercial formula or boiled animal milk as part of a diet that provides adequate micronutrient intake. Meals should be provided four to five times daily. 5. Conditions for Safe Formula Feeding: HIV-positive mothers should only use commercial infant formula as a replacement feed if specific conditions are met, including access to safe water and sanitation, reliable provision of sufficient formula, clean preparation practices, exclusive formula feeding for the first six months, family support, and access to comprehensive child health services. 6. Background on Breastfeeding and HIV: Breastfeeding is a cornerstone of child health, development, and survival, particularly in regions where diarrhea, pneumonia, and undernutrition are leading causes of child mortality. Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, followed by continued breastfeeding with complementary foods for up to two years or beyond, is the recommended feeding practice. In regions with high HIV prevalence, such as southern and eastern Africa, the use of breast-milk substitutes among non-HIV-exposed infants is associated with increased morbidity and mortality. The long-term benefits of breastfeeding for maternal and child health, including child development and prevention of non-communicable diseases, underscore the importance of supporting breastfeeding in all settings. 7. WHO Recommendations on HIV and Infant Feeding: In 2010, WHO recommended ARV interventions to prevent postnatal HIV transmission through breastfeeding. This marked a shift from individualized counseling to a public health approach, promoting one feeding practice for all HIV-positive women accessing care in public health facilities. The updated framework for HIV and infant feeding (2012) provided guidance to governments on creating environments that support appropriate feeding practices for all infants while scaling up interventions to reduce HIV transmission. 8. Lifelong ART for HIV-Positive Mothers: Since 2013, WHO has recommended lifelong ART for all HIV-positive mothers, and since 2015, for all individuals diagnosed with HIV, regardless of clinical or immunological criteria. This approach requires long-term planning, coordination, and support from national health authorities and international agencies. 9. Target Audience and Population of Interest: The guidelines are intended for national policymakers, program managers, healthcare providers, researchers, and development partners. They are particularly relevant for countries with high HIV prevalence and settings where diarrhea, pneumonia, and undernutrition are common causes of child mortality. 10. Priority Questions for Review: In 2014, WHO identified priority areas for review, including the duration of breastfeeding by HIV-positive mothers, interventions to support infant feeding practices, and guidance for mothers who do not exclusively breastfeed or plan to breastfeed for 12 months. 11. Evidence and Recommendations on Breastfeeding Duration: In settings where maternal and child health services promote breastfeeding and ART, HIV-positive mothers should breastfeed for 12 months while receiving ART, as this increases HIV-free survival compared to shorter breastfeeding durations or replacement feeding. 12. Summary of Evidence: Systematic reviews and modeling studies have shown that longer durations of ART for mothers are associated with greater HIV-free survival for infants. However, the quality of evidence is low due to the observational nature of studies and methodological heterogeneity. These detailed explanations provide a comprehensive understanding of the guidelines and recommendations on HIV and infant feeding.
